title: Right concentration
hook: the mind gathered and unified, in the four jhanas (MN 141)

segments.voice: Yesterday: makkata, and your line, don't grab the pitch. Did you catch one second grab before it happened? Day three hundred ninety-five, and the last factor of the path.

Sunlight falling on a sheet of paper does nothing much. Gather the same sunlight through a magnifying glass, and the paper starts to smoke. Nothing was added. No extra sun. The light was only collected into one point. Water from a garden hose works the same way: spread into a mist, it barely wets the grass; gathered into a stream, it reaches the far end of the yard. The eighth and last factor of the eightfold path is about that kind of gathering. Today: right concentration.
screen: `THE SAME SUNLIGHT.` → `GATHERED INTO ONE POINT.` → `NOTHING ADDED.`

segments.voice: In Pali it's samma samadhi. Samadhi is usually explained from a verb meaning to put together, to collect. The mind gathered. In MN 141, where Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, right concentration is defined simply: the four jhanas, four deepening states of meditative absorption. We'll spend the next four days on them, one at a time, with the Buddha's own pictures for each. Today is about the gathering itself, and three things are worth knowing. First, concentration in the Buddha's teaching isn't a strain. It isn't frowning hard at a point. In the suttas' own pictures of the jhanas, the gathered mind is pleasant, even joyful. Second, it's never alone. MN 117 calls it noble right concentration with its supports: the seven factors that come before it. A mind gathered to plan a burglary is gathered, too. It isn't right concentration. Third, concentration and understanding work as partners. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's translation: “Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.” Buddhist schools differ on how much concentration a person needs, and how deep. In Theravada teaching, calm, samatha, and insight, vipassana, are often described as developed together; some teachers stress deep absorption, others a lighter, moment-to-moment steadiness. Zen and Tibetan schools train the gathered mind in their own ways. The Dhammapada's own point is the pairing: knowledge and meditation, each needing the other.
screen: `SAMADHI — THE MIND GATHERED.` · `NOT A STRAIN, AND NEVER ALONE.` · `KNOWLEDGE AND MEDITATION TOGETHER.` · `SCHOOLS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `GATHERED.`

segments.voice: If you have ten minutes today, this is a good day to use them. The bell holds two; keep going when it rings, if you can. Choose one place where the breath is clearest, the nostrils or the belly, and let your attention rest there. When it scatters, gather it back gently, the way you'd sweep crumbs into your hand. No need to count the scatterings. Every gathering is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Samadhi. Concentration: the mind gathered and unified, the eighth factor of the path.
Your line: gathered. Once today, do one thing with your whole attention, the dishes, a conversation, a short walk, and notice what changes. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Buddhists across schools train concentration in meditation, often on the breath; in Theravada communities it is commonly taught as calm (samatha) alongside insight (vipassana), and Zen and Tibetan schools have their own methods for steadying the mind.

fork.setup: you sit for ten minutes and your mind scatters twenty times. what does the path invite?
options: give up: you just can't concentrate
gather it back each time; each gathering is the practice
force it to stay, jaw clenched
fork.reveal: samadhi means gathering, and gathering only happens to something that scattered. twenty returns is twenty pieces of practice.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit samādhi: from sam + ā + dhā, to put together; the mind collected.

trapdoor: what you thought: concentration, like cramming for an exam.
what it means: the mind gathered and unified, resting on the other seven factors of the path.
what a scholar hears: MN 141 defines right samādhi as the four jhānas; MN 117 defines it as one-pointedness of mind with seven supports, the other factors of the path.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 141, Saccavibhanga Sutta (right concentration as the four jhanas)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (noble right concentration with its supports)

notes: Dhammapada 372 quoted from Max Müller (1881) from memory; please check the exact wording against the 1881 text.
